cards.title: Why is this fingerprinting script creating bioweapons?

depth.text: someone found an **anti-bot script** hiding **scary prompts** and suspicious commands to **confuse AI tools**

The author crawled **10,000 websites** with Playwright and collected their canvas fingerprints at fingerprint.garden. The script’s **Node-only branch** includes commands to inspect files, gather system details, and download a binary; the author suspects this is **anti-LLM bait**, noting the file-reading callbacks do nothing.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters see this as a way to deter AI crawlers; skeptics say agents can ignore dead code, and warn that the prompts could harm customers’ brands.

cards.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5

depth.text: someone built a **CPU** inside a language model that runs code using the model's own **memory**

Qwenputer adds a **32-bit RISC-V core** to Qwen 3.5 4B; its Gated DeltaNet layers act as RAM, letting it run arithmetic, C and MicroPython inside the model without external tools. It passed the official riscv-tests and ran **18 million instructions** without a single error, but each instruction costs a few decoded tokens.

comments.text: This is fun and games, but wait until an agents finds this and does the most misaligned thing with it in order to fold paper clips. > Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too. cards.title: StackOverflow now gets fewer than 1000 questions a month

depth.text: Stack Overflow gets **fewer than 1,000 questions a month**, and commenters debate **what drove the decline**

One commenter says question numbers were already **nearly 50% down** from their June 2020 local maxima before ChatGPT, though its launch sped the drop; another blames Stack Overflow’s **hostile attitude** towards users.

cards.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model

depth.text: Claude Code sends **background agents’ transcripts** to their own model for **tiny status summaries**

The author's telemetry says agent summaries take **16.4% of spend**, versus 15.7% for the main conversation; that spend is Claude Code's per-request estimate, not an invoice. A **Bun preload** blocks the **summary timer**, so the agent-panel status stops updating.
data: agent_summary share of all Claude Code spend
main conversation share of all Claude Code spend

cards.camps: Two camps: some say cache hits make these calls cheap or their impact limited; others call the hidden usage wasteful and question providers' incentives.

comments.text: While we're modding Claude Code, Anthropic also includes your email in the system prompt, and Opus _constantly_ includes it in request headers. https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeCode/comments/1xhqvzn/opus_55... You can remove it with a claude plugin https://github.com/AlexErrant/claude-code-no-email/blob/main...

cards.title: About the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs

depth.text: Apple is **blocking compromised certificates**, but some Mac command-line tools may still **accept them**

Apple says **Safari, Mail, and apps** using its networking and security frameworks block the affected certificates automatically. Some command-line tools check **/etc/ssl/cert.pem** instead and may accept them until a future software update; administrators can remove the relevant root CA certificates sooner.

cards.camps: Two camps: critics say Apple should have fixed the file in a security update; defenders say its transparent guidance is the right approach while a software update is pending.

comments.text: > On Mac, some command-line tools included with macOS or the Xcode Command Line Tools (including curl, git, python3, ruby, perl, and openssl) check certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem. For certificates that chain to a root CA certificate in this file, these tools don't check Apple's block or whether the certificate has been revoked. This file will be updated in a future macOS update. If you…

It's wild to see people supporting this bizarre anti-security response. Not only are they dragging their feet in fixing the security issue, they're actively reverting any manual fixes silently with each new update. That's legitimately worse than doing nothing at all! It's also disconcerting to see folks advocate for the "let's wait to fix this critical security issue because we want to make it…

I'd really like to know why it's taking Apple so long to ship a fix. Especially if they can explain how to update an existing computer, what's the general holdup? Is it their release process? Is there some underlying complexity that's poorly understood?
Related: Ten days later, Git on macOS still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50271640

cards.title: Formlabs Studio 1 $699 Resin Printer

depth.text: Formlabs' **resin printer** starts at **$699** and prints most parts in **under two hours**

It accepts **nine Formlabs materials** or **third-party materials** through Open Material Mode. Alpha Resins use low-odor components, and their **UL GREENGUARD Gold** certification applies when printed on this machine with the VOC Extractor.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see a compelling beginner-friendly deal; others say resin printing is messy and recommend FDM instead.

comments.text: Formlabs uses a proprietary resin cartridge... it's the paper printers situation all over again, the printers themselves are not that expensive but the disposable ink costs an arm and a leg. Don't go with Formlabs, support any of the open-platform alternatives. And also, be aware that these printers require some serious development work (you need solvent to wash away uncured resin (if you ask me…

I have a resin printer (elegoo mars 2p) and have done a number of small "production" runs of things that don't really matter. I have to say that it is the biggest pain in the arse thing I even own. While the prints come out "good", I find that dimensional accuracy is often really not good at all; and that the whole rinse in isopropyl, finish in the sun process is just a sticky, irritating, and…

This thing is all over YouTube, they really backed up the truck to the Influencer Club and started handing out the goods. Lots of people I like and respect have showcased it, like Applied Science, Jeff Geerling, among others. But although there's a lot of discussion about how large a discount this is from FormLab's 8 billion dollar printers, there is absolutely NO comparison that I can find to…

You don't want a resin printer. They are nasty, chemically, they require you to set up a "hot zone", you need ppe, venting is really important. When your print works good, you still have to wash it and then cure it. Changing colors ids like a whole event. FDM printers are amazing now. Strongly recommend an FDM printer.
This page really needs to explain what is “resin printer” and why would I need it. I have no idea how is it different from my regular 3D printer.

glossary.canvas fingerprinting: Drawing something on a webpage’s canvas and using tiny differences in how it looks to recognize a browser setup.
glossary.obfuscation: Making something harder to see or recognize.
glossary.Node: Software that lets JavaScript run outside a web browser.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.jailbreak prompt: Text meant to trick an AI into ignoring its usual rules.
glossary.RISC-V: A processor design that sets out the basic instructions software runs on.
glossary.Gated DeltaNet: A kind of model layer that can keep information in a changing internal memory.
glossary.RAM: Random-Access Memory: a computer's working space for information it is using right now.
glossary.forward pass: One run through a model to produce an answer, rather than building it one piece at a time.
glossary.one-hot key: A way to point at one memory slot by marking just that slot in a list.
glossary.free-running: A test run where the CPU keeps going on its own, without another machine correcting each step.
glossary.local maxima: High points on a graph compared with nearby points.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.Bun: A program that lets JavaScript run outside a web browser.
glossary.preload: A file a program loads before its normal work starts, often to add or change behavior.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.cache hit: When software finds saved information it needs and can reuse it.
glossary.OpenTelemetry: A way to collect and send records about what software is doing, such as its requests.
glossary.subagent: A helper assigned a smaller part of a larger task.
glossary.rate-limit headroom: How much usage room remains before a service restricts you for using too much.
glossary.agent_summary: The label the article uses for background-agent summary requests in its usage records.
glossary.chemotherapy: Medicine used to kill cancer cells, though it can also affect healthy parts of the body.
glossary.lumbar puncture: A procedure where a needle goes into the lower back to take or replace fluid around the spine.
glossary.lymphoma: A cancer that starts in the body's infection-fighting system.
glossary.port catheter: A small device under the skin that connects to a blood vessel so medicine can go in.
glossary.PHP: PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor; a language people use to make websites work.
glossary.LTS: Long-term support: a release its makers promise to support for an extended period.
glossary.atrial fibrillation: A heart rhythm problem that can make the heartbeat uneven.
glossary.immunotherapy: Treatment that helps the body's immune system fight cancer.
glossary.certificate: A digital ID that helps show which website a connection belongs to.
glossary.TLS: Transport Layer Security: a way to scramble information as it travels between devices, so others can’t read it.
glossary.intermediate CA: Certificate authority: a service trusted to confirm website identities; an intermediate one is a middle link that can vouch for a website's certificate.
glossary.root CA: Certification Authority: the top-level organization a device trusts when deciding whether a website's certificate is valid.
glossary./etc/ssl/cert.pem: A Mac file some command-line tools use as their list of trusted certificate issuers.
glossary.resin printer: A 3D printer that hardens liquid resin with light to build a part layer by layer.
glossary.MSLA: Masked Stereolithography: a resin-printing method that uses a screen to shine light on selected areas and harden a layer.
glossary.FDM: Fused Deposition Modeling: a 3D printer builds an object by laying down melted plastic in thin lines.
glossary.VOC: Volatile organic compounds: Gases that can come from products and materials and affect indoor air.
glossary.Open Material Mode: A setting that lets the printer use materials made by other companies, not just Formlabs.
glossary.UL GREENGUARD Gold: A certification for products tested for low chemical emissions.
glossary.IPA: Isopropyl alcohol: a solvent used here to wash leftover resin off prints.
